item.title: Scott Bessent insulted Democrats. Now he needs their help to avert a debt crisis.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has spent nearly two years publicly belittling Democratic lawmakers. Soon, he'll need their help to keep the United States from descending into a fiscal crisis. The U.S. is on track to hit its $41.1 trillion borrowing limit within weeks of Democrats taking control of Congress, setting up a showdown that could come to a head as early as next summer. Bessent may have some fences to mend first. The secretary has insulted Sen. Elizabeth Warren 's intelligence, saying the next chair of the Banking Committee "knows even less about foreign exchange markets than she does about banking." He asked Rep. Maxine Waters (D-Calif.), the top Democrat on the House Financial Services Committee, to "maintain some level of dignity" after she asked the chair, Rep. French Hill (R-Ark.), to "shut him up" during a hearing. And he accused incoming Senate Finance Chair Ron Wyden 's son of being an associate of the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. "My experience with the secretary is — 'easy' is not the first word that comes to mind," Wyden, whose committee has jurisdiction over debt limit action, told reporters earlier this month. Bessent's history of personal attacks will test whether he can broker a deal between President Donald Trump and Democratic leaders before Treasury runs out of cash to pay the nation's bills. A protracted debt limit standoff, even if it ultimately gets resolved, could rattle bond markets and push up borrowing costs. Sen. Jack Reed of Rhode Island, a senior Banking Committee Democrat, was more direct about Bessent's relationship with his party: "I don't think it's very good." But the Treasury secretary has already signaled he wants to work with Democrats when they take over the House and Senate next year. At a Heritage Foundation event earlier this month, he said he would "try to take something out of the Bill Clinton-Newt Gingrich playbook" in fiscal negotiations with Congress' incoming majority — a nod to the bipartisan budget deals struck in the 1990s between the former Democratic president and Republican speaker. "Look, people like Bessent because he works hard — and he is MAGA, but he is also respected by CEOs no matter what party they are," a senior Trump administration official granted anonymity to speak candidly said in a statement to POLITICO. "The President gives him big projects, and he gets at it." A Treasury spokesperson declined to comment. For decades, action on the debt limit has spurred high-stakes standoffs on Capitol Hill over how to reverse the nation's fiscal trajectory, with the risk of default often becoming a point of leverage in partisan negotiations. Generally speaking, Democrats support "clean" debt ceiling increases while Republicans demand that they be paired with larger concessions around curbing federal spending. If Democrats don't like what they hear in talks with Bessent or other top Republicans this time around, they have other options for raising the debt limit. They could follow the GOP's example from last year and raise the ceiling through a party-line budget reconciliation package — daring Trump to sign it or risk downgrading the U.S. credit rating and spooking Wall Street investors. They could also ask Senate Republicans to agree to a last-minute deal to raise the debt limit with a simple-majority vote as they did in 2021 . Sen. Tim Kaine (D-Va.), the incoming Budget chair, described his own relationship with Bessent as "pretty much nonexistent." But taking the gavel, Kaine said, means "the relationship, by necessity, is probably going to get a little more communicative." Even some Republicans say Bessent has relationship-building to do if he wants to influence policy during the next two years. "He needs to get here," Sen. James Lankford (R-Okla.) said of Bessent in an interview last week. "Honestly, I think one of the challenges the administration will have is there just hasn't been enough relationship between the Cabinet here and Democratic members of the House and the Senate." But Lankford praised Bessent as being "very in the details. I think he'd be a good negotiator to be able to carry the president's message." Despite the public clashes, some Democrats think more highly of Bessent than of many other top Trump officials, said a Democratic lobbyist who works on financial services issues. "A lot of Democrats view him privately as someone they can work with on certain issues," said the lobbyist, who was granted anonymity to speak candidly. This isn't the first time the Trump administration has had to raise the debt ceiling under divided government; Trump's first Treasury secretary, Steven Mnuchin, negotiated directly with then-Speaker Nancy Pelosi on a 2019 deal to suspend the limit for two years. Joe Lavorgna, a former senior counselor to Bessent at Treasury who is now chief economist at SMBC Nikko, predicted a standoff over the debt limit this time around: "There's going to be a lot of brinkmanship and a lot of fighting. I hope I'm wrong, but I don't think it's going to go smoothly." Bessent will have to contend with lawmakers in both parties who want to use debt limit negotiations as an opportunity to overhaul the whole federal budget process, including potentially triggering debt limit increases and spending caps when Congress adopts a budget. "There really is a prospect of trying to make our rather feckless budget process more sensible and effective," Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.) said in a recent interview. Other Democrats now see an opening to demand an end to debt-limit standoffs for good — for instance, Pennsylvania Rep. Brendan Boyle , the top Democrat on the House Budget Committee, has a bill aimed at ending high-stakes debt ceiling showdowns by allowing Treasury to suspend the debt limit, subject to a Congressional override. Warren, meanwhile, hasn't forgotten that Trump endorsed scrapping the debt ceiling in December 2024, just weeks before he returned to office — and that Bessent, during his confirmation hearing last year, told the Massachusetts Democrat that, if Trump "wants to eliminate the debt ceiling," he would work with Congress and the president to make that happen. "This is one more place where I agree with Donald Trump. We need to put an end to it," Warren told reporters last week. It's not clear if Trump still holds this position, or if he will be able to maintain it amid pressure from conservatives to fight efforts to raise the debt ceiling without major concessions. The White House did not respond to a request for comment. Longtime congressional deficit hawks also note that many of the fiscal constraints enacted during past debt limit negotiations were overridden in subsequent years — including "pay-as-you-go" triggers for across-the-board cuts enacted in 2010 to make sure the federal government doesn't spend more than it brings in. This could harden their resolve to fight efforts to pass a "clean" debt ceiling increase next year. "The disappointing thing is everything we've ever done in the past has been abrogated and ignored," Sen. Rand Paul (R-Ky.) said in an interview, adding that he also feared Bessent could broker a debt limit deal that includes an agreement on new funding totals that would substantially increase spending next year. Sen. Rick Scott said GOP fiscal hawks will be urging Bessent to steer debt limit talks toward achieving "fiscal sanity." Asked how much room Bessent would have to negotiate a deal, the Florida Republican pointed back to the secretary's boss. "He's a hard worker. But ultimately, Trump is actually the one who's negotiating," Scott said. "There's only one president." While the United States has never defaulted on its debt, top economists have projected that reaching that point would spark a severe recession, costing the economy millions of jobs and wiping out trillions of dollars in household wealth. That kind of economic turmoil would be a stain on the legacies of congressional leaders, as well as Bessent and Trump. "We have to do it. And he should be very concerned," Reed said of Bessent. "If they don't raise the debt limit, they're going to have serious financial problems. … This has to be done. I hope he realizes that." This article originally appeared on Politico at https://www.politico.com/news/2026/11/25/bessent-debt-treasury-trump-democrats-congress-01182853

item.title: Trump says Iran war 'funded' through January until Democrats take control of Congress
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Talks between the U.S. and Iran remain stalled despite the two countries signing a memorandum of understanding in June, aimed at ending the war that began with joint American-Israeli strikes on the country in February. The opening strikes killed a host of top Iranian officials and commanders, among them Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. The two sides have continued to exchange strikes, though have not returned to the intense fighting seen in the early stages of the conflict. The U.S. says it is enforcing a naval blockade of the country's Persian Gulf and Gulf of Oman ports, while Iran claims control over the strategic Strait of Hormuz and continues to claim attacks on shipping transiting the waterway. Meanwhile, intensified fighting between Saudi-backed Yemeni forces and Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen has seen the latter repeatedly attack Saudi military, oil infrastructure and transport facilities. See the most recent developments below. Latest Developments Nov 25, 9:28 AM Renewed Yemen fighting displaces 364,000, UN official says Renewed fighting in Yemen's civil war has forced more than 364,000 people from their homes since August, including tens of thousands over the past week, the United Nations' humanitarian chief said in a statement Wednesday after he arrived in the port city of Aden in the south of the country. "Fighting, insecurity and heavy restrictions along key supply routes are preventing families from accessing the food and medicine they need to survive," UN Under Secretary General for Humanitarian Affairs Tom Fletcher said, noting that half of Yemen's population needs aid. "Millions are hungry," he added. Fletcher also called on the Houthi rebels to "immediately and unconditionally release our detained UN colleagues and other humanitarians." "Our work and our people must be protected," he said. Since 2014, Yemen's internationally-recognized, Saudi-backed government -- now based in Aden -- has been fighting with the Iran-backed Houthis, which occupy the capital Sana'a. The conflict has become a widening front in the regional war involving Iran that began in February. Mohammed Huwais/AFP via Getty Images - PHOTO: A Yemeni boy inspects the damage following a strike allegedly carried out by Saudi forces that targeted a horse farm on the outskirts of Sanaa on Nov. 24, 2026. -ABC News' Morgan Winsor Nov 25, 7:02 AM Houthis claim fresh attacks in Saudi Arabia A military spokesperson for the Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen said on Wednesday that the group launched new strikes targeting the financial district in Riyadh and a key Saudi oil refinery. In a video statement, Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree said the operation against the financial district in Riyadh "caused extensive damage." The Ras Tanura refinery in Saudi Arabia's Eastern Province was also targeted, causing "fires to break out there," Saree said. Early on Wednesday morning, a Saudi military spokesman said four drones had been intercepted in Ras Tanura and "a number of fragments fell as a result of the interception, with no casualties." Satellite images showed black smoke above the Ras Tanura oil refinery on Wednesday. Nasa Worldview/via Reuters - PHOTO: A satellite image shows a large smoke cloud billowing over Saudi Arabia's Ras Tanura oil refinery on Nov. 25, 2026. -ABC News' Nasser Atta and Othon Leyva Nov 25, 2:55 AM Trump says Iran war 'funded' through January President Donald Trump said the ongoing war with Iran is "funded" through January, when Democrats take control of Congress and could reign in his authority to authorize the conflict. In an interview with the New York Post conducted in the Oval Office on Tuesday afternoon, Trump said the incoming Democratic majority will "take a total win and make it a loss." Trump again touted the U.S. military success against Iran. "Their navy's gone, their air force is gone, their anti-aircraft, everything's gone. Their leaders are gone. I mean, if [Democrats] do that, they'll just take a win and make it a loss," Trump said. When pressed on whether his timeframe to freely launch renewed strikes is narrowing, Trump reportedly said he finds it "hard to believe" that Democrats would stop the war. "I don't know how they could do that politically, because we have a win. We can put that war to bed anytime we want," Trump said, according to the Post. Israel's goal of ending the Islamic Republic is "probably doable," Trump also said, but told the Post that regime change is not his goal. "I just don't want them to have a nuclear weapon. I was never for or against regime change, that was never a criteria for me," Trump said. Trump also addressed an Iranian announcement this week that it would be suing the U.S. for compensation for an airstrike on a school. "Well, I want compensation for the people that they've killed, which is far more because they've killed, first of all, they killed 75,000 protesters in the last seven months. But they've killed our people for years," Trump replied, according to the Post. "The USS Cole, they've killed many, many hundreds of Americans. So if they want to play the compensation game, we win," the president said. -ABC News' Isabella Murray Nov 24, 11:49 AM US investigating whether Iran is behind tanker cyberattacks The U.S. is investigating whether Iran is behind a series of cyberattacks that targeted energy tankers, according to multiple officials. At least 50 ships are believed to have been attacked, with some receiving bomb threats that purported to say the ship was to be detonated. The U.S. has identified Iran as the prime suspect, but are also investigating whether Russia could also be the suspect. The threats are believed to scare boats into not traversing overseas. The Coast Guard has helped thwart all of the cyber attacks, according to officials. They've also posted a warning on their website telling tankers to patch their systems, prior to a cyber event occurring. "Just as we monitor for mechanical or weather-related hazards, we incorporate cyber risk management into our routine, professional approach to facilitating commerce and ensuring safe vessel transits into and from our ports and waterway," according to a Coast Guard spokesperson. Earlier this year, two boats headed to Texas were boarded by U.S. Coast Guard teams after it was discovered that cyber incidents occurred onboard. Nov 24, 9:11 AM Riyadh tower targeted in attack, Saudi spokesperson says A tower in the financial district of the Saudi capital Riyadh was targeted in a "terrorist attack," a Saudi military spokesman said Tuesday. "One of the towers of the financial center was targeted in a cowardly terrorist attack," Maj. Gen. Turki al-Maliki, the spokesman for Saudi-led coalition forces fighting the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen, posted on X. The post did not provide details about the nature of the attack. One of the towers in the Riyadh financial center was damaged last week when it was hit by a projectile. -ABC News' Othon Leyva Nov 24, 9:03 AM UKMTO reports attacks on 3 tankers in Strait of Hormuz on Monday The United Kingdom Maritime Operations (UKMTO) Centre on Tuesday issued a warning after it received a report of three vessels being struck by projectiles in the Strait of Hormuz on Monday evening. The vessels were reported to have continued their transit with all crew members accounted for, UKMTO said. Separately, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Navy on Tuesday claimed that several tankers hit naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz, the Islamic Republic News Agency reported. The IRGC Navy said the vessels were traveling through the strait "illegally." The IRGC has repeatedly claimed vessels have been damaged by naval mines, but U.S. Central Command has called previous claims false. -ABC News' Othon Leyva Nov 24, 6:27 AM Iranian army chief threatens 'unimaginable' response to any new infrastructure attacks Army chief Maj. Gen. Amir Hatami said on Tuesday that any resumption of U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iranian infrastructure would be met with "unimaginable" retaliatory infrastructure attacks. "We have now developed new operational plans to implement these new strategies and have made the necessary preparations," Hatami said, as quoted by the semi-official Mehr News Agency. "Should our infrastructure be struck again, we will strike their infrastructure in a way that is not easily reversible," he added. Nov 24, 4:09 AM Ship attacked off UAE on Sunday, UKMTO says The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) Centre on Tuesday confirmed that a bulk carrier was hit by an "unknown projectile" while at anchor off the coast of the United Arab Emirates on Sunday. The incident occurred 23 nautical miles northeast of the Emirati east coast city of Khor Fakkan, the UKMTO alert said. "A fire was reported onboard the vessel but no casualties have been reported at this time," the alert said. Nov 24, 3:43 AM US land blockade of Iran 'impossible,' Araghchi says Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Monday that the proposed U.S. land blockade of his country "is impossible, both because of the country's vastness and the large number of provinces." U.S. Central Command announced earlier this month the formation of Task Force Iron Gate, which would be assigned "to prevent Iran from using ground routes to transport advanced weapons and other materials." In comments published by the IRIB state broadcaster on Tuesday, Araghchi said Iran's "extensive connections with neighboring provinces in neighboring countries, high traffic and people-to-people ties, and historical and cultural roots on both sides of the border," meant that the U.S. task force would fail. "There are capacities in the country's provinces, especially the border provinces, that can open what the enemy wants to close to us," he added. "The duty of the country and the people is to discourage the enemies from imposing sanctions; the best way to counter these pressures is to discourage the sanctions takers from achieving their goals so that they know that this tool is not and will not be effective," Araghchi said. "Of course, this does not mean abandoning the other duty of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, which is to open diplomatic channels for negotiations and lifting sanctions, and that path is also ongoing," he continued. -ABC News' Desiree Adib Nov 23, 6:49 AM Trump says Iran launched more attacks in past week than at any time 'for over a year' President Donald Trump said in a social media post on Sunday night that "Iran has launched more drones and missiles in the last week than at any time for over a year." "Don't worry, they've all been knocked down, and done no damage," Trump said of the Iranian attacks. Reported attacks in and around the Strait of Hormuz have been higher in number in October and November than any previous months since the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran began in late February, according to data compiled by maritime organizations and analyzed by ABC News. Iranian forces have also been launching fresh missile and drone attacks on regional nations like Kuwait and Bahrain. -ABC News' Isabella Murray Click here to read the rest of the blog. This article originally appeared on Good Morning America at https://abcnews.com/International/live-updates/iran-live-updates-tehran-strait-hormuz-safe-demands/?id=138369648

item.title: A share of Anthropic now costs less than a copy of 'GTA 6'
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Was it better to hold exposure to this year's record-breaking IPO or what may be the biggest entertainment launch in history? The two collided last Thursday when AI giant Anthropic's ( ANT ) initial public offering hit the market just as Rockstar Games officially released "Grand Theft Auto VI." So far, the video game trade has come out ahead for investors. Shares of Rockstar's parent company, Take-Two Interactive ( TTWO ), are up more than 5% since last Thursday. Anthropic, meanwhile, was trading about 6% below its IPO price in premarket trading on Wednesday, after closing below it for the first time on Tuesday. It is also trading below the $79.99 cost of a standard copy of “GTA VI” in premarket trading Wednesday. Take-Two ( TTWO ) said last Friday that "GTA VI" churned out $3.79 billion in global sales on its first day, describing the video game release as "the biggest entertainment launch in history." Anthropic's record IPO, which raised roughly $81 billion before any exercise of the underwriters' additional-share option, has quickly shifted from first-day enthusiasm into a tricky debate over a range of factors that may be responsible for the stock's lackluster performance, including insider stock sales, how the IPO launch process was executed, and whether the company's enormous revenue growth prospects can overcome its massive computing commitments. The speed of the reversal from the new company's 17% first-day gain is notable. Among the 12 biggest US IPOs since 2008, only Uber ( UBER ) and Facebook, now Meta ( META ), broke their IPO prices sooner , according to Yahoo Finance calculations. By comparison, it took about a month before shares in this year's other monster IPO, rocket maker SpaceX ( SPCX ), slipped below its IPO price of $135. SpaceX's stock is down more than 7% from that level as of Tuesday. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said earlier this month that the company hoped to "underpromise and overdeliver " in its public launch. During the same interview at JPMorgan Chase's Manhattan headquarters with CEO Jamie Dimon, Amodei laid out the immense promise he believes his firm's AI models could one day have not only for investors but humanity. His vision included the hope AI could one day help make cancer, heart disease and other terminal illnesses "relics of the past." Many investors still remain bullish on the AI firm's promise too. "I do believe this could be the first $10 trillion company," Madhu Namburi, a managing director at General Catalyst and former veteran tech dealmaker for JPMorgan, told Yahoo Finance's Deirdre Bosa on Monday. The "Grand Theft Auto VI" game case is seen on a table on Nov. 19, 2026, in New York City. (Photo illustration by Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images) Michael M. Santiago via Getty Images Follow David Hollerith on X @DsHollers . This article originally appeared on Yahoo Finance at https://finance.yahoo.com/technology/article/anthropic-and-grand-theft-auto-vi-launched-on-the-same-day-the-video-game-trade-is-winning-for-now-171431006.html

item.title: Russia's own leaked records show almost 500,000 military deaths in war in Ukraine
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Russia does not provide numbers of its fallen soldiers [AFP via Getty Images] At least 490,334 Russian soldiers have died since the start of the war in Ukraine in 2022, according to Russian government statistics analysed by the BBC. The leaked Rosstat data reveal how the full-scale invasion of Ukraine has fundamentally changed mortality patterns in Russia, and show the high cost paid in human life in a war that Vladimir Putin had assumed would last only days but is now almost five years old. BBC Russian has had access to more than 11 million death records from 2021 to September 2026, after a hack by Belarusian group Cyber Partisans BY and Ukraine's Silent Crow. Russia's statistics agency admitted to a cyber-attack, but denied any protected information had been leaked. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on Wednesday that only Russia's defence ministry could officially report data on losses: "I suggest no other data be taken into account." The defence ministry has not released any official casualty figures for several years. Together with independent Russian outlet Mediazona, BBC Russian has compared the Rosstat data with its own list of confirmed military deaths, pulled from open sources since the start of the invasion, and it has found matches for 90% of the records. Military experts estimate that the BBC's list of 290,012 deaths, gleaned from official reports, social media, new memorials and graves, may account for 45-55% of the true death toll, which would range from 527,295 to 644,471. The records show that 65% of 18 to 24 year-olds in Russia who lost their lives in 2025 died in the war. For those aged 25-34 the number was 59%. Only among 45 to 54 year-olds does cardiovascular disease claim more Russian lives than the conflict. The data also reveal the extent of losses in specific areas of Ukraine. Some 20,000 Russian soldiers died fighting for control of 10 Ukrainian villages whose combined pre-war population was 12,000. During the fight for one small village called Andriivka, south of the town of Bakhmut in Donetsk region, 1,122 Russians lost their lives. Before the war 74 people lived there. Russia does not give public figures for losses sustained since the war began in February 2022. And two years ago Rosstat stopped publishing data of deaths from external causes, which was used to gauge the extent of military losses. For example, only 70% of deaths we have established of soldiers from the occupied regions of Donetsk and Luhansk in eastern Ukraine who fought in the Russian army were accounted for in the Rosstat files. Overall, the Rosstat dataset confirms the trends that we have observed with our own count. Ukrainian losses were last put at about 50,000 by President Volodymyr Zelensky in July 2026, but another list based on open sources by the anonymous UA Losses website puts the figure at 115,952. How we came to a figure near half a million The Rosstat dataset contains no names but does include ages, places of residence, places of death and also circumstances of death. We have filtered the records first by location, leaving only Ukraine as well as Russian border regions that saw incursions by the Ukrainian army. Next, we identified 425,174 entries explicitly indicating a military-related cause of death, such as explosions or shrapnel during combat operations. As this count could include civilians, we filtered out women as well as men outside the 18-65 age group. And if someone lived and died in the four Ukrainian regions occupied by Russia, we excluded them as a possible civilian – unless he had a record of military service attached to his entry. Another 14,093 entries were identified by looking at employment, and 51,067 were recorded in the database as deceased on the basis of a court ruling. This often happens when a soldier goes missing in a combat zone for more than six months and their body has not been recovered. Again, we filtered out civilians by only counting deaths in the war zones in Ukraine and Russia. According to BBC Russian's analysis of the leaked files, in the first year of the war the average age of those killed was 34. By 2025, as prisoners and contract soldiers entered the ranks, it had risen to 40 (38 according to our own list). Some of Russia's poorest regions in Eastern Siberia account for a disproportionately large share of the losses. Men from Tyva, Buryatia and Zabaykalsky Krai are 20-25 times more likely to die in the war than residents of the biggest cities of Moscow and St Petersburg. [AFP via Getty Images] In most regions, the distribution of deaths based on Rosstat data differs from that in the BBC's list by just a few tenths of a percentage point. At least 5,017 foreigners are among those who died fighting for Russia, according to our analysis of the Rosstat files, including 1,031 Uzbeks and 720 Tajiks. We have left out Ukrainians from this count to avoid including civilians. This is a conservative estimate as dual nationals are listed as Russians in the database, and there is no reference to North Koreans who died repelling the Ukrainian incursion into Russia in 2024. The BBC identified 2,304 North Korean soldiers who died there by analysing satellite imagery and official photographs of a newly built memorial in Pyongyang. The leaked Russian statistics may not be complete but taken in conjunction with BBC Russian's own work they are significant. In the context of a war that has lasted four years and 10 months, these are high numbers for Russia, when compared with the Soviet war in Afghanistan that ended in 1989. In that 10-year war, an estimated 15,000 Red Army troops died, and an estimated one million civilians were killed. item.title: How the FAA's new Line Up and Wait rules may impact Thanksgiving holiday air travel
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The Federal Aviation Administration imposed new standards for its Line Up and Wait airport policy on Tuesday that, though not a significant change, could affect travelers during the busy holiday travel season. Line Up and Wait (LUAW) is a procedure that allows planes preparing for departure from busy airports to taxi into position on the runway while they wait to be cleared for takeoff. It’s designed to make airport departures more efficient by putting planes in position to take off as soon as airspace has been cleared. Under the FAA’s new policy , airports can still use LUAW, but they must designate a watch supervisor whose sole job is to oversee LUAW operations and whose attention cannot be split by other tasks. The new rules change guidance from saying that airports “should” have a dedicated LUAW supervisor to saying that they “must” have one. The FAA said the change is intended to “elevate the safety standard” for LUAW operations by “removing ambiguity” about staffing requirements under the old rules. Will the new rules affect Thanksgiving holiday travel? The impact of the policy change on passengers comes down to staffing. At airports with enough staff to assign one person exclusively to LUAW, the effect will likely be minimal. But airports that may be short-staffed, a chronic problem in recent years, might be unable to use LUAW. That could mean slightly longer waits on the tarmac in some cases. Even minor delays caused by the new LUAW policy could be compounded by potential disruptions from the Thanksgiving travel rush , with 417,000 flights expected to depart during the 9-day holiday travel period and stormy weather forecast for both coasts. The new LUAW rules will also be in place for the December holiday travel season. They are scheduled to expire in June. FAA under scrutiny Though the new policy represents a relatively minor procedural update, it comes at a time when the FAA is under intense scrutiny following the historically disruptive nationwide ground stop that resulted in the cancellation of 18,000 flights earlier this month. That outage, plus a series of smaller technical disruptions in the weeks since, has fueled a sense of “outage anxiety” among holiday travelers. In a recent YouGov poll, 72% of respondents said they were concerned about "flight cancellations or significant delays as a result of further disruptions to U.S. air travel" over the holiday travel season. Nearly a third said the ground stop could potentially lead them to alter their travel plans. The new LUAW rules are not related to the ground stop or other recent disruptions. They were first proposed in early October, more than a month before the ground stop occurred. There were no reports of significant delays related to the new rules on Tuesday, the first day they were in effect and the busiest day of the Thanksgiving travel season. Congress is debating whether to provide the FAA with billions of dollars in additional funding to upgrade its infrastructure and implement other changes to prevent future outages. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy has asked for $50 billion , but even lawmakers who support a funding boost for the FAA say the final price tag could be much smaller. The debate could affect LUAW operations at the nation’s airports, depending on whether Congress approves funding to help them address staffing shortages that may limit their ability to assign someone exclusively to LUAW. This article originally appeared on Yahoo Travel at https://travel.yahoo.com/news/article/new-faa-rule-line-up-and-wait-impact-on-thanksgiving-holiday-air-travel-174323076.html

item.title: Inflation remains high despite retreating gas prices, highlighting challenges for the Fed
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The Federal Reserve's preferred inflation gauge showed prices heated up more than expected in October, all but guaranteeing the central bank will raise interest rates next month, with the prospect of further hikes in the first quarter. The "core" Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) index, which strips out volatile food and energy prices, picked up steam last month, rising 3.3%, compared with expectations for 3.2% and up from 3.1% in September. Month over month, core prices held steady at 0.3%, in line with projections. On a headline basis, PCE was in line with expectations for 3.8%, up from 3.6% in September. Month over month, PCE moderated, rising 0.3% as expected and down from 0.5% previously. "The continued strength in core PCE inflation … make[s] a December rate hike certain," said Bradley Saunders, economist for Capital Economics. "While we still think a 25bp hike is the most likely course of action at next month's meeting, the strength of the data means a follow-up hike in January could also be necessary." Sauders noted that the latest data boosted the three-month annualized rate of inflation to 3.6%, from an upwardly revised 3%. Core goods price pressures almost doubled to 0.35% month over month, as energy prices continued to feed through, taking the annual rate to 2.3%, from 2%. Services price growth was also strong, up 0.28% month over month, led by recreational services and food and accommodation services. But Mike Skordeles, head of US economics for Truist Advisory Services, isn't too alarmed by Wednesday's report, noting that the comparisons from last year's data were much lower, making the numbers look hotter. Skordeles expects the same trend to continue in November, as both headline and core were equally below trend in 2025. "The overall inflation trajectory is largely unchanged, especially when excluding food and energy," said Skordeles. Most Fed officials have already coalesced around a rate hike next month, though some have called for more aggressive action than others. Wednesday's report may seal that action for some members. Read more: How to protect your savings against inflation Fed governor Chris Waller said that if the central bank hikes by a quarter point next month, it will need to signal a follow-up hike of the same size in January — or else deliver a jumbo half-percentage-point increase in December. Fed governor Lisa Cook echoed that urgency on Friday, arguing that financial conditions remain too accommodative while inflation remains stubbornly high. She warned the central bank risks falling behind the curve if it doesn't hike now. New York Fed president John Williams, however, has pushed back against calls for supersize rate hikes , saying last week that he doesn't think the situation calls for "dramatic action." Williams said earlier this week that the Fed needs to take a more forward-looking approach to inflation and thus to setting rates, noting that monetary policy works with a lag of one to two years to have its maximum effect on the economy. His statement that the Fed needs to be more forward-looking does not align with its approach in recent years. The central bank has tended to be data-dependent, which is inherently more backward-looking. Williams didn't suggest that the Fed not consult data, but rather that any actions taken today will take a year or two to be implemented. But new tariffs being proposed of up to 20% on China, the EU and 12 other nations could boost inflation. One reason Williams has been sanguine about the inflation outlook is he believes tariffs have largely washed out of the picture. However, he's also said that would change if new tariffs were put in place. The administration's latest proposal could mean new tariffs take effect early next year, pending comments, hearings and further negotiations. That raises the prospect of further rate hikes and holding rates higher for longer. Follow Jennifer Schonberger on X @Jenniferisms and on Instagram . item.title: Sean Hannity has outlasted Fox rivals. Now he's eyeing the GOP's future.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
WEST PALM BEACH, Fla. – America had swung to the left with a historic rebuke of President Donald Trump, and Sean Hannity wished it was still Nov. 5, 2024. Instead of another Trump win, it was Nov. 3, 2026, and Hannity, the face of Fox News since the network’s inception 30 years ago, could only joke on air: He wasn’t going to flee to Ireland like a certain Trump nemesis now that Democrats had won the biggest congressional landslide in 50 years. Besides, he was only 10 days removed from his splashy Mar-a-Lago wedding weekend festivities to Fox News host Ainsley Earhardt – and now was not the time for a honeymoon or a move. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. “Hatred is a hell of a motivator,” he concludes of the Democratic turnout. Since Election Day, this kingmaker for the political right has been trying to reason on air that midterms can be predictable for presidents with dominant personalities, but nothing about Texas going blue is cyclical. While the MAGA fever appears to have broken, there is a silver lining for Hannity: The Hannity Primary to help decide the next Republican presidential nominee is about to begin. Nov. 7, 2028, has been on Hannity’s mind. He plans to interview every Republican presidential candidate on his show, guessing that Vice President JD Vance, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) would be among the favorites. There are three questions he will pose to the contenders: Are you a conservative? Can this person appeal? Will the coalition be broad enough so that person can win? These are the same questions he asked of Trump during “very long, late-night, deep conversations about every topic imaginable” in the early days of his long-shot 2016 campaign. “I was very straight with him,” Hannity says from the brown leather chair on his podcast set, “and said, ‘If you don’t convince me, I’m not going to vote for you, and I will not support you.’ Period.” When Hannity liked the answers, he became Trump’s most influential and dependable ally in the mainstream media in the decade that reshaped American politics. Republicans muscling their way to the 2028 nomination don’t necessarily need Trump. What they really need is the support of Hannity and what he did for Trump. “You could be the perfect conservative, but if you don’t have the ability to win a race, why would I support you?” he asks, adding that Trump was “the right man in the right place at the right time with the right personality.” At 64, Hannity is many things to the generations who’ve heard and seen him rise from Long Island kid and college dropout to one of the most prominent and most hated conservative voices on radio and TV over the last three decades. To his allies, he is the standard-bearer of conservative talk radio whose shows on TV and radio remain essential to understanding this extended MAGA era of American life. Even at a time when Fox’s leading ratings have taken a sizable hit - including a 27 percent drop in total viewers last month compared to October 2025 - Hannity, the longest-running cable news host in history, consistently ranks among the top-five cable news programs nationwide in both viewers and in the coveted 25-54 demographic. Forbes has estimated his annual salary from Fox at about $25 million. To his critics, Hannity is despised for using his vast media empire to peddle poisonous propaganda in defense of Trump and his agenda. In 2017, he heavily promoted the false conspiracy surrounding the murder of Democratic National Committee staffer Seth Rich, despite no evidence linking Rich as WikiLeaks’ source of hacked DNC emails. Fox News eventually retracted the story and agreed to pay millions to Rich’s family to settle out of court. Asked to comment, a Fox spokeswoman sent the network’s statement from the time that it hoped the settlement “enables Mr. and Mrs. Rich to find a small degree of peace and solace moving forward.” Hannity had also repeatedly amplified Trump’s false claim that his 2020 election loss to Joe Biden was rigged. Before Fox News settled the defamation lawsuit brought by Dominion Voting Systems for $787.5 million, Hannity said in a sworn deposition that he did not believe Trump’s false claim that the election was stolen “for one second.” A Fox spokeswoman said that Hannity testified he had aired the claims to allow for proof to emerge. “Him promoting the Seth Rich conspiracy theory was really disgusting, and illustrated his place in the MAGA era,” says Oliver Darcy, a veteran media reporter and the founder of the Status newsletter. Nicole Hemmer, a political historian at Vanderbilt University, and the author of “Messengers of the Right: Conservative Media and the Transformation of American Politics,” adds that Hannity survived both incidents when other hosts wouldn’t because “he’s made Fox News much more money than they ended up paying.” “The audience has really developed a taste for these deep conspiracies, and he was serving it up,” she says. Hannity prefers to point to a list of stories that he claims he was right about when other mainstream journalists dismissed him, from the innocence of Richard Jewell at the 1996 Olympics to the investigation of Russian interference in the 2016 election. “We’ve been vindicated more times than I can count,” he claims, defiantly. To watch Hannity on TV is to see a relentless, right-wing messenger and tastemaker whose opinions you know you’ll never be able to change. Even when he might be wrong, he knows he’s right. As the last remaining prime-time anchor from Fox News’s original 1996 lineup, Hannity has survived an abysmal beginning to his career, low ratings, advertiser boycotts and flashier opinion hosts who’ve come and gone - Glenn Beck, Bill O’Reilly, Tucker Carlson. “Sean is very good about people and their needs, their understanding of politics and culture, and he moved with that,” says Fox News host Laura Ingraham, a longtime friend who credits Hannity for urging her to join the network. “Sean is both just a really good analyst and entertainer because you have to engage people in these topics.” Hannity’s steadfast support of Trump has continued in the president’s second term, such as on a recent episode of his Fox show when scrolling graphics touted Trump’s alleged “Top Accomplishments.” “We talk on the phone all the time,” Hannity says, but insists he can keep his personal relationship with the president separate from his professional one. Critics say there’s almost no daylight whatsoever between Trump and Hannity. But ESPN host Stephen A. Smith has a different take on what his close friend has meant to Trump: “I don’t think Trump would have become president without Sean.” “If Sean Hannity is in your corner, you won’t find someone more doggedly in support of you than him,” Smith continues. “You’re going to have to go through him and a ton of brick walls he puts up to get to his friends. Because come hell and high water, he’s gonna do everything that he possibly can do to protect the people that he supports and he cares about. It’s who he is, for better or worse.” “I’ll let other people make that judgment,” Hannity says, adding of Trump, “We still have a personal relationship. I’ll put it that way.” Now, as Fox News celebrates its 30th anniversary this fall, Hannity is reflective about his life and career, namely his place in media, the Trump era, and his future. Would he entertain leaving Fox when Trump exits the White House more than two years from now? Of course not. If you haven’t been paying attention for the last 30 years, Hannity is not going anywhere - and suspects that his monologues would continue in his car once he eventually signs off. “It would not be a good look if I stopped at a light - ‘Who is that crazy guy talking to himself? Is that Sean Hannity?’” he says. “But I’m not planning on talking to myself anytime soon.” Today he is talking to Rahm Emanuel, former White House chief of staff, former Chicago mayor, current Democratic presidential aspirant. “We can be nice and ease our way into open warfare,” says Emanuel, before the cameras start rolling for the taping of “Hang Out with Sean Hannity,” or “we can go nuclear.” On the podcast set in West Palm Beach with a refined man-cave aesthetic featuring brown liquor, a neon sign, pool table, samurai swords and a signed Matthew Tkachuk Olympic hockey jersey, Hannity flips through a thick stack of stapled, printed-out notes before the taping begins. It’s how he arms himself to go to battle with Emanuel for the next two hours. They joust about the Obama years, the Chicago years, the ambassador to Japan years - and whether Emanuel should run for president. I don’t think you can get nominated. Ambassador is a bulls--- [title], let’s be honest. You have your memory, and then I have the facts. Stepping into Hannity’s world is a road game for Emanuel, but he gets his shots in, too. “As always,” he says of Hannity, “you tell half the story.” After the pair is finished dropping verbal bombs on each other’s heads, they pose for an I-guess-we-will-take-a-photo-together photo to commemorate the marathon taping. Hannity is relieved but not tired. “I know Rahm’s a smart guy,” the host acknowledges afterward, “but there was no way I was coming into this interview today not prepared.” Sean Patrick Hannity was not always this prepared, not when he was a bigmouthed kid with strong opinions who smoked cigarettes in between innings of Little League games he was pitching. He loved his parents for eventually instilling a strong work ethic in him, even if his father beat him with a belt whenever he got sideways. A two-time college dropout, he worked in restaurants, construction and started his own house-painting business in Rhode Island, before moving to Santa Barbara, California. It was there, in his late 20s, that he began hosting a talk-radio show at KSCB-FM, the volunteer radio station for the University of California at Santa Barbara. He discovered that talking in front of a microphone was what he wanted to do for the rest of his life. He also discovered what could get you fired: Less than a year in, he was sacked for casting doubts about the AIDS epidemic and telling a lesbian mother that he felt bad for her child. He later admitted his comments were “ignorant and embarrassing.” Hannity used his firing as self-promotion, framing himself as “the most talked about college radio host in America” and a budding conservative shock jock. He worked at radio stations across the South until Roger Ailes came calling to pluck Hannity from obscurity and put him on the ground floor of a new cable network called Fox News. Hannity was terrible - truly terrible. When he was paired in a nightly talking heads duel with liberal co-host Alan Colmes for “Hannity & Colmes” in 1996, the first review was so rough that he remembers it verbatim three decades later. Alan Colmes looks funereal; Sean Hannity has a bad haircut and has no business being on TV. “I asked management once why they didn’t fire me,” he says. “They said, ‘Well, nobody was watching, and we knew you were a broadcaster and that you would get it.’” The higher-ups were right. Hannity became the cable-news authority on what the conservative base was feeling and thinking, Ingraham says. “The appeal of him is he is the comfort watch: You know exactly what you’re getting almost all the time with him,” Hemmer says. Darcy adds, “Some people come up fast and burn out really fast, but Sean is just there .” The highs were high when Hannity went solo with his own show in 2009; the same viewers who had tuned in to watch Hannity steamroll Colmes now wanted Hannity to steamroll everyone, even if he wasn’t always the funniest or most photogenic personality on the network. But his audience began to shrink in the early 2010s, and moving his show from 9 p.m. to 10 p.m. hurt even more. The tea party movement had fizzled, and the GOP lacked a true leader. Reports were also swirling that Fox would change its direction, and that Hannity was on his way out after the Rich debacle sparked advertiser boycotts. Then, something happened: Trump, the real estate mogul and “The Apprentice” host had, in Hannity’s eyes, become a fun character who would be great for the political contest because of his outspokenness and enthusiasm. That is, if the billionaire ever decided to run for president. When Trump did, Hannity and Ingraham became the first and most emphatic at Fox to put their full weight behind him in 2016. “I was on the night before [the election] with him, and he looked at me and said, ‘Hell, we better be right about this or else we have to change our names and move to South America,’” Ingraham recalls. “Donald Trump would have been fine on his own,” says Dan Bongino, the radio host and former FBI deputy director, “but I think he would tell you himself that having Sean onboard early was definitely helpful in the start of what became this MAGA movement, which I believe a lot of people hope even outlasts President Trump.” Hannity’s style is a throwback to the conservative talk-radio ecosystem of the ’90s where he was created: fast-talking and confrontational, passionate and provocative, and above all, hyper-partisan. Compared to segments featuring liberal guests and Democrats, which can feel like an anything-goes barroom brawl, his interviews with Trump officials and Republicans are largely seen as casual catchups with friends. Which is why in the wake of a brutal and fleeting inaugural press briefing, White House press secretary Katie Zacharia retreated to Hannity’s show, where she believed she would find a soft landing and a chance to reset. But when the segment began, Hannity grilled her about her legal education and why the briefing was so short. When the interview concluded, Zacharia was left wondering what the hell had just happened. She was fired the next day, lasting just five days in the job. “The overt hostility was unexpected considering I was President Trump’s hand-selected press secretary,” Zacharia says to The Washington Post of Hannity. “Even a hostile anchor would likely not have treated me with such animosity.” When asked about the segment, Hannity maintains it was not “a sanctioned hit by the president,” saying, “I was not trying to attack her in any way. But I knew as the interview was going on, I’m like, ‘Uh oh, you’re not putting this to rest at all,’” he says. “Her next briefing, if she had one, would have been a disaster, in my humble opinion. And I don’t wish that on anybody.” Hannity says he’s at a point in his life where he’s no longer upset about conservative or mainstream media members sniping at him, but that doesn’t mean he’s going to forget, either. There’s Ben Shapiro and Glenn Beck, who “spent three years of their life kicking the crap out of me on their radio shows, and saying I’m not a real conservative.” There’s Tucker Carlson, who told NPR in September about how Hannity had fallen into a ratings trap and “doing the same show every night because it worked three years ago … don’t do that.” “I’m not going to take advice from a guy who got fired from NPR, CNN, MSNBC and Fox News,” Hannity says of Carlson, noting that they got along when he was at Fox. “I wish him the best in his career, but if I wanted career advice, he would not be the guy to go to.” (Carlson did not respond to an interview request.) He has other ways to spend his time. Krav Maga workouts. Florida Panthers hockey. And, most importantly, Earnhardt, 50, who he had been quietly dating when Vanity Fair broke news of the relationship in 2020. The couple married in October in Palm Beach, Florida, where Hannity moved himself and his studio permanently in 2024. It was his second, her third, sealed with a lavish series of celebrations attended by a guest list thick with boldface names from the administration and Fox News. Lee Greenwood performed. The bride and groom both wore white. The weekend began with a Mar-a-Lago pre-wedding reception that Trump and first lady Melania Trump attended. The president did not offer any marriage advice, Hannity says, still hoarse three days after the festivities. And Trump also didn’t pipe up again with the advice he had given Rupert Murdoch years before: Mr. Murdoch, why do you even pay him? He’ll do it for free . “I’m looking at him like, ‘Can you please be quiet? You don’t have to tell him,’” the host recalls. “I don’t get much friend time with him anymore. I can easily bifurcate my professional role with him and my personal role with him. Not everyone has that, I understand, and there are critics of that, and I’m fine with that, too. “But I’m not being dishonest with my audience, at all, about any of it.” It seems spot-on for a man who follows the news obsessively and texts his producer story and monologue ideas at all hours of the day and night. Soon, one of those ideas will be the beginning of the Hannity Primary, and the 2028 Republican presidential candidates will go on the show to try to win arguably the most important Republican blessing on prime-time TV. “I felt Donald Trump could win,” he says, “and I was not wrong.” Related Content This article originally appeared on Washington Post at https://washingtonpost.com/style/2026/11/25/sean-hannity-has-outlasted-fox-rivals-now-hes-eyeing-gops-future/

item.title: Trump's intervention to get Jensen Huang reinstated was about more than Nvidia
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
At the center of the White House's push to get Jensen Huang reinstated as CEO of Nvidia was a conviction that he plays a critical role in keeping the artificial intelligence sector competitive. According to a source familiar with the matter, President Trump and Vice President Vance view Huang as a vital defender of open-source AI models — which offer users greater control, customization, privacy, and cost flexibility — and believe his leadership is necessary to prevent closed-source AI developers from consolidating power. Trump and Vance worked through the weekend to bring Huang back. After behind-the-scenes persuasion from the White House, Nvidia's board staged a stunning reversal Monday, returning Huang to the CEO position. Prior to the reinstatement, the president and vice president were briefed on the national security dimensions of the situation. Both concluded there was no evidence Huang had engaged in any illegal or improper conduct regarding US national security. According to the source, Trump believes maintaining a close working relationship with Huang offers the administration the strongest opportunity to safeguard national security and prevent advanced chips from reaching prohibited buyers. Trump said during a CNBC interview Monday that Nvidia's board had sought assurances that Huang did not pose a national security threat due to his ties to Alice Huang, a Singapore-based Megaspeed executive suspected of links to Chinese intelligence with whom he had an affair. Huang resigned on Nov. 12 after acknowledging that and other extramarital affairs, but was reinstated after just 12 days. In a post on Truth Social on Monday, Trump urged the company to maintain strict oversight, writing, "NVIDIA should continue its thorough internal investigation of the Company's compliance with U.S. export controls in order to ensure that it is fulfilling its legal obligations and Patriotic Duty to protect U.S. National Security." Trump also noted that his assessment aligned with the Justice Department's. A Justice Department official confirmed that Attorney General Todd Blanche spoke with the president over the weekend, and that the department has found no evidence of wrongdoing by either Huang or Nvidia. Addressing reporters at a press conference Tuesday, Blanche said, "To the extent that the Department of Justice had information that he was committing crimes or something like this, that's something that I would have certainly told the president had it been true," when asked whether Huang had been investigated. Blanche neither confirmed nor denied investigations into any diversion of Nvidia chips to China, only noting that investigations are always happening and he can only say so much publicly. Blanche called Nvidia a "good corporate citizen," noting that if it were subject to a criminal investigation or were obstructing the Justice Department, Trump would not have told the American public that the US government does not possess evidence that Huang engaged in any unlawful conduct. "I have no reason to stand up here and say Nvidia is anything but a good corporate citizen directly to the board of directors," said Blanche. Nvidia surged more than 30% on Monday, nearly reclaiming the losses following Huang's resignation. The stock skidded nearly 6% Tuesday to $155.38. Nvidia stock fell more than 5% during premarket trading on Wednesday. There are still myriad unanswered questions, including whether Nvidia's latest Blackwell chips were routed via Singapore's Megaspeed to China. Huang will face both closed-door and public sessions with lawmakers in Washington next week to discuss exactly what happened. Follow Jennifer Schonberger on X @Jenniferisms and on Instagram . item.title: Immigrants fear holiday travel amid ongoing ICE crackdowns
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Immigrants facing detention by federal authorities are making hard choices about whether Thanksgiving travel is worth the risk, advocacy rights groups say. More than 81 million people plan to travel at least 50 miles from home for the holiday, according to AAA. But the Trump administration's aggressive immigration enforcement efforts, highlighted in part by the Nov. 21 detention of two people at the Seattle-Tacoma Airport, has some people reconsidering their movements. That includes immigrants with the legal right to live and work in the U.S. but who want to avoid being stopped and questioned, said Zachary Mueller, a senior strategist with the advocacy group States at the Core. "Some people are terrified to leave their house," said Mueller, whose organization has trained about 75,000 people to monitor and record ICE detentions. "For some people, that fear has become so palpable in day-to-day life that this holiday is nothing new on that level." Mueller added: "For others, they're asking 'is traveling to go see family for the holidays worth the risk of never seeing my family again?' That's a real calculation." The exact number of people facing deportation is unclear, but roughly 350,000 Haitians and about 600,000 Venezuelans lost Temporary Protected Status in the past two years. The Department of Homeland Security reports that in fiscal year 2026, ICE carried out more than 483,000 deportations, the most ever in a single year. President Donald Trump has promised the largest mass deportation in U.S. history, and during his second term DHS reports that more than 3 million people have already left the United States either via deportation or self-removal. Immigrants who leave the United States voluntarily can receive a $3,000 payment and a free flight to their home country. Administration officials said they will continue to enforce immigration laws, including those that make it harder for undocumented immigrants to fly. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers routinely check Transportation Security Administration manifests for potential immigration violators. Last May, the Department of Homeland Security began requiring flyers to show REAL ID-compliant identification to board airplanes, a move that made it easier to detect people who lacked permission to live in the United States. People without REAL ID can fly but are subject to additional security checks and may have to pay a $45 fee. “DHS reversed the horrendous Biden-era policy that allowed aliens in our country illegally to jet around our country. Under President Trump, DHS will no longer tolerate this," an unnamed DHS spokesperson said in a statement. "This administration is working diligently to ensure that aliens in our country illegally can no longer fly unless it is out of our country to self-deport." Immigrants who are considering travel should check first with their attorney and make sure to carry copies of relevant paperwork, said Krish O’Mara Vignarajah, the president and CEO of Global Refuge. She said many refugees who sought safety in the United States are now worried about being targeted by the same government that asked them to fill out paperwork and register their home addresses. She said many refugees, including those from Haiti and Venezuela are frustrated because Trump keeps saying ICE is targeting the "worst of the worst." "These are people who did everything right, went through vetting, did all the paperwork," she said. "And now they're asking us whether following the rules has somehow put them more at risk." Mueller said the harsh enforcement tactics also have impacts on travelers who witness anonymous and masked federal agents grabbing screaming people at airports. He said driving may not be a safe option for some people, particularly if they are driving through communities that have signed cooperative agreements allowing local police to help enforce immigration laws. "It's not just the people who are first affected, but that kind of fear and trauma and concern, the wanton separation, the ability of ICE to do whatever it wants and create these chaotic scenes ... millions of Americans have been seeing this," Mueller said. "They're asking themselves when they travel, 'am I going to see something that's going to ruin my holiday because this administration wants to rip apart families?' That's the absurd reality of this moment." Marjory Wentworth, a board member of the Haitian Support Center in Springfield, Ohio, said her family is hosting a handful of Haitians for Thanksgiving. Many members of Ohio's Haitian community lost their Temporary Protected Status in July. The Trump administration has revoked their work permission and urged them to leave the United States. Wentworth said none of the Haitians she knows will risk flying. She said at last one local church hosted a Thanksgiving dinner for Haitian congregants over the weekend, allowing them to celebrate without traveling far from home. "People can't go work, they've got ankle monitors," she said of her own invited guests. "I feel like people are still pretty fearful. I'm hoping we can distract them for a day." item.title: Oil prices rise after alleged Houthi attack on Saudi refinery
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
By Nicole Jao and Anna Hirtenstein NEW YORK, Nov 25 (Reuters) - Crude oil prices rose more than 1% on Wednesday after Yemen's Houthis said they had attacked Saudi Arabia's largest oil refinery and traders weighed Middle ‌East supply disruptions against the prospect of a global market surplus. Brent crude futures were up $1.80, or 1.97%, at $93.2 ‌a barrel by 12:04 p.m. EST (1704 GMT). US West Texas Intermediate crude futures climbed 96 cents, or 1.17%, to $83.01. Both benchmarks gained more than 2% ​on Tuesday. Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis said on Wednesday that they had attacked Saudi Arabia's Ras Tanura oil refinery and Riyadh's financial district. The refinery, Saudi Arabia's largest, is part of a complex that also serves as a major export terminal for Saudi crude. The Houthi statement triggered Wednesday's price rally, said PVM oil analyst Tamas Varga, citing a rising geopolitical risk premium. Traders are also likely to be covering ‌short positions ahead of the US Thanksgiving ⁠holiday, which could add to the momentum, Varga said. US CRUDE STOCKS RISE US crude stocks rose by 1.1 million barrels to 418.9 million barrels in the week ended November 20, data from Energy Information Administration showed. ⁠That compared with analysts' expectations in a Reuters poll for a 1.5 million-barrel rise. [EIA/S] The build in crude stocks was mainly due to weaker crude exports while imports rose, said Bob Yawger, director of energy futures at Mizuho. Prices also drew support from uncertainty about OPEC's 2027 policies ​ahead ​of its November 29 meeting, especially with the United Arab Emirates ​no longer restricted by OPEC+ policies and Iraq seeking ‌higher oil output capacity, said Zhenqiang Seto, an oil research specialist at LSEG. OPEC+ ministers will hold a series of meetings on November 29 to decide on their 2027 output policy. "Since the release of an IEA report this month, perceptions of a global supply glut have kept prices in check," said Tsuyoshi Ueno, senior economist at NLI Research Institute. Attention is also focused on how next year's production quotas will be determined at the OPEC+ meeting, Ueno added. Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said ‌OPEC+ is set to complete a review by year end of member ​production capacities. Iraq and Kazakhstan were pressing OPEC+ to raise its estimate of their ​oil production capacity, said four people familiar with the ​matter, heightening tensions over a review that will help determine how much members can pump next ‌year. In other supply news, Libya's Sharara oil pipeline has ​reopened. Flows were halted when a ​valve was closed by what the National Oil Corporation described as an unlawful group. Oil is again flowing into storage tanks at the Akakus facility in Zawiya, NOC said. In the Strait of Hormuz, a container ship was ​targeted and came to a stop on ‌Tuesday while sailing an "unauthorised" route near the strait, Iran's Revolutionary Guards told state media. item.title: 2 men charged after reported break-in at Prince William and Kate’s country home
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
U.K. police have charged two men over a suspected break-in at Prince William and Kate's country home. Two Albanian nationals, Mirgen Doku, 34, and Arilen Ndoci, 32, were charged with burglary and trespass after police were called to Anmer Hall, in Norfolk, England, on Monday night after reports of "suspicious activity" on the estate. The family wasn't home, Norfolk police confirmed in a statement to Yahoo. Prince William and Kate were instead thought to be at Forest Lodge, their main home near Windsor Castle, where they stay while their three children are at school in the local area. Police said in a statement Tuesday, "Two men have been arrested on suspicion of burglary following an incident at a property on the Sandringham Estate last night (Monday 23 November). Police were called just before 6 p.m. following a report of suspicious activity at the address. Officers attended and specialist resources, including police dogs, drones and the National Police Air Service helicopter, were deployed to assist with searches in the area. "Two men were arrested on the estate on suspicion of burglary and trespass. They remain in police custody. The property was unoccupied at the time of the incident. Inquiries remain ongoing." Kensington Palace said it would not comment on security matters. Anmer Hall on the Sandringham Estate in King's Lynn, England. Max Mumby/Indigo via Getty Images Anmer Hall is Kate and William's country home, located on King Charles's private Sandringham Estate. It's a vast 10-bedroom property that was given to the couple as a wedding present from Queen Elizabeth II in 2011. They used it as their primary home during the COVID-19 pandemic and now spend Christmas and other holidays there, enjoying privacy, peace and outdoor activities. The family spends the majority of their time at Forest Lodge, which is about 20 miles west of central London and a 15-minute drive from Prince George's new $85,000-a-year boarding school , Eton College. His younger siblings, Princess Charlotte and Prince Louis, attend Lambrook, a coeducational private school an eight-minute drive from the house. Forest Lodge is an ideal location for the family to be based, as William and Kate can easily reach the U.K. capital, where many of their public engagements take place. Today, William met with U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham at Burnham's London home and office, 10 Downing Street. Kate, meanwhile, is awaiting the airing of her upcoming documentary, Heal. The "deeply personal" documentary covers Kate's diagnosis, recovery and life beyond cancer. It will be broadcast in the U.S. on Nov. 30 at 8 p.m. ET/PT on NBC, on Bravo at 11:30 p.m. ET/PT, and will be available to stream on Peacock from Dec. 1. item.title: Army official says all 5 tons of lead azide were successfully destroyed in Iowa
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The U.S. Army detonated 5 tons of unstable bomb-making chemicals as part of a controlled explosion on Wednesday morning, despite a legal battle over the potential health and environmental impacts from the dust. The explosion detonated the nation's entire stockpile of lead azide, a highly sensitive explosive material, at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant. The Army has released maps showing where the dust could drift and warned people to avoid the area, adding that children under 6 and pregnant women are particularly vulnerable to lead exposure. The detonation followed an appeals court decision that found adequate safeguards to protect the community were in place. Officials have been taking steps to mitigate the risk, such as barriers around the blast zone. In leaflets handed out to local residents, the Army said the chemicals had degraded, becoming "extremely unstable and sensitive to even slight friction or movement" — meaning there is a risk of an explosion if they attempt to move or store the chemicals any longer. The Environmental Protection Agency said it had granted an emergency permit to detonate 68 drums of the lead azide because a "controlled detonation during optimal weather conditions and incorporating robust mitigation measures, compared to an uncontrolled explosion, significantly reduces the potential reach and concentration of lead dust landing on surfaces, such as homes and windows." Officials in Missouri and Illinois are also monitoring the situation . item.title: NASA deliberately crashed into an asteroid. Now scientists are surveying the damage.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The asteroid before (left) and after, showing the crater left behind by a spacecraft's impact [ESA] The first images of an asteroid that Nasa deliberately crashed into have revealed a stadium-sized crater on its surface. The extensive damage was caused when a Nasa spacecraft hit the asteroid Dimorphos in 2022. The asteroid posed no threat, but this was a test of our planetary defences to see if it was possible to knock a space rock off course. Four years on, a European Space Agency (ESA) spacecraft called Hera is scouring the scene to fully assess the aftermath of the collision. "The crater is almost as large as the body itself, which is really, really spectacular," said Dr Sabina Raducan, a planetary scientist, who is on the Hera science team. "It's hard to describe in words all the excitement to actually finally see what happened. And as a crater person, I can also say it's beautiful." The original 2022 crash test was carried out by a Nasa spacecraft called Dart which hurtled into Dimorphos at 14,000mph (22,000km/h). It was such a big smash-up that the trail of debris, measuring about 6,200 miles long (10,000km), was spotted by telescopes on Earth and in space. Dimorphos is about 150m (500ft) wide and was partly chosen as the target because it is one of an asteroid pair - it orbits around a larger space rock called Didymos, which is about 730m (2,400ft) wide. The crash showed it was possible to change the path of the smaller asteroid. Before the collision, it took Dimorphos 11 hours and 55 minutes to orbit around Didymos. After the crash, the duration of its orbit had shrunk by about 33 minutes. The mission has sent back new pictures of the smaller Dimorphos orbiting around Didymos [ESA] The Hera spacecraft's arrival on the scene is helping scientists answer many more questions. Not only did the collision alter the shape of Dimorphos, it also changed the way it moves. "Before the Dart impact, Dimorphos was more like our own Moon - so it was always showing the same face to Didymos, and it was behaving quite nicely," explained Raducan. "Now it's very, very chaotic - it's tumbling. Imagine a barrel that you throw down the stairs, and the barrel is rolling and it's moving, and basically that's what Dimorphos does right now around Didymos." Hera has also taken detailed images of Didymos, revealing its surface in detail. "The gravity at the surface of Didymos is about 40,000 times less than the gravity on Earth," said Naomi Murdoch, who is on the Hera mission team. "We can already see some fascinating and complex geology. We can see regions of boulders. "The smallest details that we can make out in these images are about 3m in size. So that means that all the boulders that you can see with your eyes are at least 3m big, and some as big as 10m. So what we're seeing here is boulders the size of cars and buses sitting on a world with almost no gravity." A long trail of debris from the collision was spotted by the Hubble Space Telescope [NASA/Hubble Space Telescope] The Hera mission will spend the next six months studying Dimorphos and Didymos, sending back more images taken from closer up in higher resolution. "Hera is a sort of Inspector Columbo going back to the crash scene to investigate what is the outcome of this impact," said Patrick Michel, principal investigator of ESA's Hera mission. The spacecraft is packed with instruments and also has two shoe-boxed sized satellites onboard, which can study the impact site up close, and then later land on the asteroid. But the first images taken by Hera have also revealed a new challenge. Dimorphos and Didymos are travelling through space surrounded by hundreds of boulders ranging in size from tens of centimetres to metre-size rocks. This will make it especially challenging to operate the spacecraft and cube satellites through this boulder field. A key task is to measure the mass of Dimorphos, in order to work out how effective the spacecraft's shove was. This information would be vital if we ever spotted a space rock that was on a collision course with Earth. "It would help us to predict what would happen if we had to hit another asteroid," said Prof Simon Green, a planetary scientist who is on Hera's science team. "We [could] measure its properties and say: 'Well, we need this mass of spacecraft, travelling at this speed, this early, in order to deflect it enough so that it misses the Earth'." This was the last image from Dart before it crashed into Dimorphos in 2022 [NASA/Johns Hopkins APL] Asteroids pose a significant threat to our planet. The biggest, which measures more than a kilometre across, could cause global devastation. But medium-sized asteroids around the same dimensions as Dimorphos could wipe out a city. "We all know what happened to the dinosaurs, right? And we don't want that to happen to us," said Carolyn Ernst at Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory, who has worked on both the Dart and Hera missions. "The good news for us is that there are far fewer potential threats out there in the Solar System than there were millions of years ago. But there are objects out there." She said the biggest asteroids have been spotted, and none are heading to Earth. "The smallest stuff isn't too much of a threat because our atmosphere protects us," she added. "But there's a size range in the middle where we don't know where all of them are, and it could, if impacted, cause problems for humanity. And if we can find out about that and know about that, well, we sure as heck would want to try to stop that." Artist's impression showing Hera. It has two small satellites on board to study the asteroid up close [ESA] Scientists want to gather as much intelligence as they can about space rocks to make us as well equipped as possible to deal with whatever the Universe throws at us. A new mission is launching in 2027 to track potentially hazardous asteroids - a space telescope called the Near-Earth Object (NEO) Surveyor. There are also more visits planned to asteroids, including to one called Apophis, which is about 450m (1,480ft) long. Apophis was discovered in 2004 and it was initially thought it might hit the Earth as early as 13 April 2029. But now scientists understand its orbit better, and say it won't hit us for at least the next 100 years. Instead of a crash in 2029, it will fly just 32,000km (20,000 miles) above our surface. This will give scientists the rare chance to study a space rock up-close. Two spacecraft will head to Apophis, including Nasa's Osiris-Apex (which previously grabbed a sample from another asteroid called Bennu) and Ramses, a joint mission between ESA and the Japanese Space Agency (JAXA).
